lessonInput.title: Lithosphere and mantle convection
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection. Claim 1: Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge. Claim 2: At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.
lessonInput.readings: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 1.5, BCcampus Open Education

claims: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection.
Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge.
At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

anchors.quote: solid rock, but is plastic enough to be able to flow slowly
new lithosphere forms (at ocean ridges), and the plates move apart
one plate will be subducted (pushed down) into the mantle beneath the other

attribution: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 1.5, BCcampus Open Education

facts: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection.
Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge.
At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

keyTerms.df: Lithospheric plates are rigid structures that move above slowly flowing solid mantle rock.
keyTerms.eg: At convergent boundaries, one lithospheric plate can be subducted beneath another.
keyTerms.mi: The rigidity of lithospheric plates means they cannot move above mantle rock.
keyTerms.cx: Rigid plates do move over mantle material that flows slowly while remaining solid.

keyTerms.df: Mantle convection is sustained by heat transfer as solid mantle rock flows slowly.
keyTerms.eg: Heat transfer sustains mantle convection beneath moving lithospheric plates.
keyTerms.mi: Mantle convection requires mantle rock to stop being solid.
keyTerms.cx: The moving mantle material retains its solid state as it flows slowly.

keyTerms.df: Ocean ridges are settings where upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere as plates diverge.
keyTerms.eg: At ocean ridges, new lithosphere forms while plates move apart.
keyTerms.mi: Ocean ridges are convergent boundaries where one plate is subducted beneath another.
keyTerms.cx: These ridges coincide with upward mantle flow and plate divergence.

scenario.su: A mapper must label a boundary represented by upward mantle flow at an ocean ridge and plates diverging. The available labels distinguish ocean-ridge lithosphere formation from convergent-boundary subduction, so the mapper must choose one despite the shared involvement of mantle and plates.
scenario.ma: Students compare the ocean-ridge observation showing upward mantle flow and diverging plates, the convergent-boundary passage describing one plate subducted beneath another.

mc.q: A comparison notes that rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock while heat transfer sustains mantle convection; which proposition preserves the distinguishing behavior of the mantle rock?
op: Solid mantle rock can flow slowly
Rigid lithospheric plates can flow slowly
Mantle convection moves above rigid lithospheric plates
Heat transfer sustains rigid lithospheric plates
mc.ex: Mantle rock remains solid yet can flow slowly beneath moving rigid lithospheric plates. Slow flow describes the mantle rock, not the rigid plates.

mc.q: A mapper observes upward mantle flow at an ocean ridge while plates diverge and must choose between lithosphere formation and subduction; which interpretation fits the recorded case?
op: Upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere
Diverging plates subduct beneath one another
Ocean ridges mark convergent plate motion
New lithosphere causes upward mantle flow
mc.ex: At ocean ridges, upward mantle flow helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge. Subduction instead describes one plate descending beneath another at convergent boundaries.

facts: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection.
Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge.
At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

keyTerms.df: These plates represent the uppermost layer of the Earth that moves above mantle rock which remains solid yet can flow slowly.
keyTerms.eg: The movement of rigid lithospheric plates is observed when tracking tectonic plate boundaries.
keyTerms.mi: Rigid lithospheric plates are entirely stationary and do not move relative to the mantle.
keyTerms.cx: The movement of rigid lithospheric plates is defined by their motion above mantle rock that flows slowly.

keyTerms.df: Mantle convection is the process sustained by heat transfer that drives the slow flow of mantle rock.
keyTerms.eg: Heat transfer sustains mantle convection as evidenced by the slow movement of mantle rock.
keyTerms.mi: Mantle convection is a rapid, turbulent process involving the immediate movement of all mantle rock.
keyTerms.cx: Mantle convection is the process sustained by heat transfer that drives the slow flow of mantle rock.

keyTerms.df: A subducted plate is one plate that can be subducted into the mantle beneath another at convergent boundaries.
keyTerms.eg: A subducted plate is observed when one plate is subducted into the mantle beneath another.
keyTerms.mi: A subducted plate is only formed when plates diverge at ocean ridges.
keyTerms.cx: A subducted plate is one plate that can be subducted into the mantle beneath another at convergent boundaries.

scenario.su: A geologist observes a divergent boundary where oceanic plates are separating, noting that the upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere. The constraint is that the observed flow rate is significantly slower than expected for rapid plate movement.
scenario.ma: Compare the observation that upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere while plates diverge with the observation that rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection.

mc.q: Distinguish between the movement of rigid lithospheric plates and the process of mantle convection based on their respective roles in sustaining Earth's dynamics.
op: Rigid plates move above solid rock while convection sustains heat transfer.
Mantle convection moves plates while rigid plates remain stationary.
Rigid plates sustain convection while convection moves the plates.
Convection moves plates while plates sustain convection.
mc.ex: Rigid plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly, while heat transfer sustains mantle convection. At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

mc.q: A tectonic setting shows a convergent boundary where one plate is subducted into the mantle beneath another, and the constraint is that the subduction process is occurring at a convergent boundary. Which observation best describes the relationship between the subducted plate and the mantle?
op: The subducted plate melts completely into magma.
The subducted plate is subducted into the mantle beneath another plate.
The subducted plate moves above the mantle rock.
The subducted plate remains solid beneath the mantle rock.
mc.ex: At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted into the mantle beneath another.

lessonInput.title: Natural experiment
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data. Claim 1: The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change. Claim 2: The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

claims: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.
The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

anchors.quote: a policy change or external event that affects one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data
whether the two groups were comparable apart from the change
the difference can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor

facts: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.
The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

keyTerms.df: A natural experiment estimates a causal effect from observational data using a change that affects one group but not another.
keyTerms.eg: A policy change affecting one group but not another is used with observational data to estimate a causal effect.
keyTerms.mi: A natural experiment requires the policy change to affect both groups.
keyTerms.cx: Its defining comparison has the change affect one group but not another.

keyTerms.df: A causal claim is credible when the compared groups were comparable apart from the policy change or external event.
keyTerms.eg: A causal claim is treated as credible when the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
keyTerms.mi: A causal claim makes the two groups comparable apart from the change.
keyTerms.cx: Group comparability supports credibility; it is not produced by making the claim.

keyTerms.df: A confounding factor is distinguished from the policy when group comparability supports attributing the effect to the policy.
keyTerms.eg: When the groups are comparable, the effect is attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor.
keyTerms.mi: A confounding factor receives the policy attribution when group comparability holds.
keyTerms.cx: With comparability, attribution goes to the policy rather than the confounding factor.

scenario.su: An analyst observes a policy change affecting one group but not another and must decide whether the estimated effect can be attributed to the policy. A deadline requires a decision while the comparability of the groups remains disputed.
scenario.ma: policy-change record identifying the affected group, observational-data comparison of the estimated effect, group-comparability assessment covering conditions apart from the change

mc.q: A natural experiment records a policy change affecting one group but not another, while a comparison shows group comparability; what distinction supports the causal claim?
op: Causal effect estimates the natural experiment
Natural experiment estimates; comparability supports causal credibility
Group comparability follows from causal credibility
Causal claim establishes comparability between groups
mc.ex: The unequal exposure identifies the natural-experiment comparison, while group comparability supports the causal claim's credibility. The causal claim does not establish comparability; comparability must support its credibility.

mc.q: A policy affected one group but not another, and records show the groups were comparable apart from the change; what decision about the observed effect is supported?
op: Treat the causal claim as creating comparability
Attribute the effect to the policy
Attribute the policy to a confounding factor
Attribute comparability to the observed effect
mc.ex: Because the records establish group comparability apart from the change, the effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor. The causal claim does not create group comparability.

facts: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.
The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

keyTerms.df: A natural experiment is a method that employs a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.
keyTerms.eg: A policy change affecting only one region's economic growth.
keyTerms.mi: A natural experiment is any study that uses observational data to find a causal link.
keyTerms.cx: A natural experiment specifically requires a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another.

keyTerms.df: A causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.
keyTerms.eg: A claim about policy impact is credible only if the groups were comparable except for the policy.
keyTerms.mi: A causal claim is always credible if the data shows a statistically significant difference between the groups.
keyTerms.cx: A causal claim is only credible if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.

keyTerms.df: The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.
keyTerms.eg: Comparability holds when the only difference between groups is the policy change.
keyTerms.mi: Comparability apart from the change means the groups must be identical in every way except the policy.
keyTerms.cx: Comparability apart from the change means the two groups were comparable apart from the change.

scenario.su: A researcher observes a sudden change in tax law affecting only small businesses in one state while large corporations in another state remain unaffected. The researcher must decide whether the observed change in business revenue is due to the tax law or pre-existing differences between the two business sectors.
scenario.ma: Compare the revenue data for small businesses in State A and large corporations in State B to determine if the causal claim is credible.

mc.q: Distinguish between a natural experiment and a standard observational study based on the required conditions for a credible causal claim.
op: A natural experiment uses observational data to find a causal effect.
A standard observational study requires a policy change for credibility.
A natural experiment requires groups to be comparable apart from the change.
A standard observational study is credible if groups are statistically different.
mc.ex: The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change, which is supported by the fact that the causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change, and a natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.

mc.q: Given the requirement for comparability, which condition must hold for the effect to be attributed to the policy rather than a confounding factor?
op: The effect is attributed to the policy if the groups are statistically different.
The effect is attributed to the policy when comparability holds.
The effect is attributed to the policy if the policy change is the only factor.
The effect is attributed to the policy when the groups are comparable apart from the change.
mc.ex: The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds, which is supported by the fact that the effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

lessonInput.title: Objects and classes
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance. Claim 1: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. Claim 2: Individual objects created from a class are called instances. Claim 3: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

anchors.quote: In a Python program, a class defines a type of object with attributes (fields) and methods (procedures)
A class is a blueprint for creating objects
Individual objects created of the class type are called instances
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object and serves as its blueprint.
keyTerms.eg: A class is used as the blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is an individual object created from a blueprint.
keyTerms.cx: The created individual is an instance; the class supplies the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: Objects are entities built from a class, with each one called an instance.
keyTerms.eg: Objects created from a class are individual instances.
keyTerms.mi: Objects define the methods shared by every instance.
keyTerms.cx: The class defines the shared methods, while objects are built from that class.

keyTerms.df: Instances are individual objects whose attributes are carried as their own copies.
keyTerms.eg: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes.
keyTerms.mi: Instances define the methods that the class shares.
keyTerms.cx: Methods come from the class and are shared by its instances.

scenario.su: Students must classify a class and two objects as either a blueprint or instances before a deadline. They must also distinguish the separate attribute copies from the methods shared by both objects.
scenario.ma: class passage stating that it is a blueprint for creating objects, object passages identifying two individual objects created from the class, attribute observation showing each instance carrying its own copy, method observation showing class-defined methods shared by both instances

mc.q: When a class is observed defining a type and an object is observed being built from it, which comparison correctly distinguishes the exact terms class and instance?
op: Class is blueprint; built object is instance
Class is instance; built object is blueprint
Instance is blueprint; class is built object
Object is class; blueprint is instance
mc.ex: The class is the blueprint, and an object built from it is an instance. Calling the instance the blueprint reverses the stated relationship.

mc.q: Two objects each carry separate attribute copies but use methods defined by their class; under a complete-comparison constraint, which account fits these observations?
op: Instances copy attributes and share class methods
Instances carry their own attribute copies
Instances share attributes and copy class methods
Class methods are shared by instances
mc.ex: Each instance has its own attribute copy, while the class-defined methods are shared by the instances. Saying attributes are shared and methods copied reverses both relationships.

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
keyTerms.eg: A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is only a set of instructions for creating objects.
keyTerms.cx: A class is a blueprint for creating objects because it defines a type of object with attributes and methods.

keyTerms.df: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
keyTerms.eg: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
keyTerms.mi: Instances are the blueprints used to construct new classes.
keyTerms.cx: Individual objects created from a class are called instances because they are the actual objects built from the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
keyTerms.eg: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
keyTerms.mi: Methods are unique to each instance and not shared across objects.
keyTerms.cx: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance because they are defined by the class blueprint.

scenario.su: A developer needs to create a system for managing different types of vehicles, requiring a structure that defines common properties and actions. The constraint is that the system must allow multiple distinct vehicle records to exist simultaneously, each with unique identification numbers.
scenario.ma: Compare the structure of a class definition for a 'Car' versus an instance of that class, noting how attributes and methods are handled.

mc.q: When a class is used as a blueprint, what is the resulting entity that is built from it?
op: The blueprint itself
The class definition
An object instance
The set of methods
mc.ex: Individual objects created from a class are called instances, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: If a class defines attributes and methods, how are the methods related across different objects created from that class?
op: Each instance carries its own copy
Methods are unique to each instance
Methods are shared by every instance
Methods are defined only by the blueprint
mc.ex: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: Synovial joints
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion. Claim 1: A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity. Claim 2: Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

claims: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion.
A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity.
Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

anchors.quote: Synovial joints allow for smooth movements between the adjacent bones
A key structural characteristic for a synovial joint that is not seen at fibrous or cartilaginous joints is the presence of a joint cavity
Ligaments support the joint by holding the bones together and resisting excess or abnormal joint motions

facts: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion.
A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity.
Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

keyTerms.df: A joint cavity is a key structural feature of a synovial joint.
keyTerms.eg: The fluid-filled joint cavity is identified in a synovial joint.
keyTerms.mi: The joint cavity holds bones together and resists abnormal motion.
keyTerms.cx: Holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion describes ligaments, not the joint cavity.

keyTerms.df: Ligaments are supporting structures that hold bones together and resist abnormal motion.
keyTerms.eg: Ligaments support a synovial joint during smooth motion.
keyTerms.mi: Ligaments are the fluid-filled cavity of a synovial joint.
keyTerms.cx: The fluid-filled cavity is the joint cavity; ligaments provide support by restraining abnormal motion.

keyTerms.df: Synovial fluid is one component listed for common movable synovial joints.
keyTerms.eg: A synovial joint includes synovial fluid with articular cartilage.
keyTerms.mi: Synovial fluid supports joints by holding bones together.
keyTerms.cx: That supporting relation belongs to ligaments, while synovial fluid is a listed joint component.

scenario.su: A student must classify a common movable joint from a notation describing a fluid-filled joint cavity and supporting ligaments. The decision is constrained to distinguishing the cavity observation from the ligament observation before the deadline.
scenario.ma: fluid-filled joint cavity notation, supporting ligaments observation, common movable joint description

mc.q: A comparison records a fluid-filled joint cavity and ligaments resisting abnormal motion; which distinction correctly assigns these two observed properties to the exact lesson terms?
op: Ligaments are fluid-filled; joint cavity resists abnormal motion
Joint cavity holds bones; ligaments contain synovial fluid
Joint cavity resists abnormal motion; ligaments hold bones
Joint cavity is fluid-filled; ligaments resist abnormal motion
mc.ex: The joint cavity is fluid-filled, while ligaments resist abnormal motion. Assigning resistance to the joint cavity reverses the stated ligament relation.

mc.q: A reviewer must label a joint by the deadline and observes a fluid-filled joint cavity plus ligaments holding bones together; which notation most directly supports a synovial joint classification?
op: Ligaments are the fluid-filled joint cavity
Synovial fluid resists abnormal motion
Joint cavity holds bones together
Fluid-filled joint cavity supports synovial joint label
mc.ex: A fluid-filled joint cavity is a key structural feature of a synovial joint. Holding bones together describes ligaments, not the joint cavity.

facts: Synovial joints are common movable joints with a joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and supporting ligaments that allow smooth motion.
A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity.
Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

keyTerms.df: A precise subject definition with at least forty characters describing the internal space of a synovial joint.
keyTerms.eg: The joint cavity is the space within a synovial joint that contains synovial fluid.
keyTerms.mi: The joint cavity is the area where bones meet without any internal fluid or cartilage.
keyTerms.cx: The joint cavity is the specific fluid-filled space within a synovial joint that is a key structural feature.

keyTerms.df: A different precise subject definition with at least forty characters detailing the tissue found within a synovial joint.
keyTerms.eg: Articular cartilage is the tissue present within a synovial joint that facilitates smooth motion.
keyTerms.mi: Articular cartilage is the hard bone structure that forms the outer boundary of a joint.
keyTerms.cx: Articular cartilage is the specific tissue within a synovial joint that allows for smooth motion.

keyTerms.df: A third precise subject definition with at least forty characters explaining the role of ligaments in synovial joints.
keyTerms.eg: Supporting ligaments are the structures that support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.
keyTerms.mi: Supporting ligaments are the fluid within the joint cavity that lubricates the joint surfaces.
keyTerms.cx: Supporting ligaments are the structures that support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion.

scenario.su: A patient presents with chronic pain in the knee, and an inspection reveals a noticeable space between the femur and tibia. The constraint is that the assessment must focus only on the structural components of the joint.
scenario.ma: Femur-tibia articulation record, observation of joint space width measurement, synovial fluid presence notation

mc.q: When comparing the structural components, which feature is specifically identified as a key structural feature of a synovial joint?
op: The presence of supporting ligaments holding bones together
The existence of a fluid-filled joint cavity
The function of articular cartilage for smooth motion
The commonality of movable joints with a joint cavity
mc.ex: A key structural feature of a synovial joint is a fluid-filled joint cavity, while the other options describe functions or general properties.

mc.q: A clinician observes a joint where bones are held together and abnormal motion is resisted; what structural element is this?
op: The joint cavity containing synovial fluid
The articular cartilage facilitating smooth motion
The supporting ligaments holding bones together
The commonality of movable joints with a joint cavity
mc.ex: Ligaments support synovial joints by holding bones together and resisting abnormal motion, which distinguishes them from the cavity or cartilage.

lessonInput.title: Comparative advantage
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything. Claim 1: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone. Claim 2: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

claims: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

anchors.quote: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill

facts: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

keyTerms.df: Opportunity cost is the distinguishing basis used to identify which producer has comparative advantage in a good.
keyTerms.eg: For a good, the producer with the lower opportunity cost has comparative advantage.
keyTerms.mi: The producer better at making everything must hold the comparative advantage in every good.
keyTerms.cx: Being better at everything does not prevent another producer from holding comparative advantage through a lower opportunity cost.

keyTerms.df: Total output is an outcome that rises when producers specialize according to comparative advantage and then trade.
keyTerms.eg: After each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and trades, total output rises.
keyTerms.mi: Trade makes total output fall after producers specialize according to comparative advantage.
keyTerms.cx: Following comparative-advantage specialization with trade raises production rather than reducing it.

keyTerms.df: Absolute skill is the property of being better at making everything, which differs from having a lower opportunity cost.
keyTerms.eg: Another producer may be better at making everything while a producer still has comparative advantage in a good.
keyTerms.mi: Differences in absolute skill are the source of gains from trade.
keyTerms.cx: Trade gains arise from differences in opportunity cost rather than from who is better at making everything.

scenario.su: A policy analyst must decide whether two producers' records support comparative-advantage specialization and gains from trade. The decision is due before a deadline, while one producer is better at making everything but the opportunity-cost entries favor the other producer for a good.
scenario.ma: opportunity-cost table for each good, specialization notation for each producer, total-output measurements before and after trade, consumption records for trade and production alone

mc.q: Records show one producer has lower opportunity cost for a good while another is better at making everything. Which comparison identifies comparative advantage and distinguishes the source of gains from trade?
op: Absolute skill, not lower opportunity cost
Absolute skill differences produce trade gains
Lower opportunity cost, not absolute skill
Better at everything means comparative advantage
mc.ex: Comparative advantage and gains from trade are grounded in differences in opportunity cost. Being better at making everything does not make absolute skill the source of trade gains.

mc.q: Two producers specialize according to comparative advantage and then trade; records show higher total output and consumption beyond production alone. Which sequence should the analyst record despite the deadline?
op: They specialized by absolute skill, then traded
They specialized by comparative advantage, then traded
They specialized by comparative advantage
They traded, then specialized by comparative advantage
mc.ex: The observed rise in total output and consumption beyond production alone follows specialization according to comparative advantage and then trade. Specialization alone omits the trade required by the supported sequence.

facts: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

keyTerms.df: A producer possesses comparative advantage in a good when they can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
keyTerms.eg: Producer A has a lower opportunity cost in producing widgets than Producer B.
keyTerms.mi: Comparative advantage means one producer is simply better at making everything.
keyTerms.cx: Comparative advantage is specifically about the lower opportunity cost in producing a particular good.

keyTerms.df: The lower opportunity cost is the measure used to determine which producer holds the comparative advantage in a specific good.
keyTerms.eg: Producer A's lower opportunity cost in widgets dictates their comparative advantage.
keyTerms.mi: Lower opportunity cost is the same as having absolute skill in production.
keyTerms.cx: Lower opportunity cost is a relative measure of production efficiency based on trade-offs.

keyTerms.df: Gains from trade arise from differences in opportunity cost between producers, not from absolute skill differences.
keyTerms.eg: The difference in opportunity cost between producers generates gains from trade.
keyTerms.mi: Gains from trade are simply a result of absolute skill differences in making goods.
keyTerms.cx: Gains from trade stem from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

scenario.su: Producer A specializes in good X because they have the lower opportunity cost for it, while Producer B specializes in good Y. This specialization allows both producers to achieve a higher total output and consume more than they could individually.
scenario.ma: Producer A's production record shows a lower opportunity cost for good X than Producer B's record, and Producer B's output record shows a higher total consumption level after trade.

mc.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the source of gains from trade between two producers?
op: Gains arise from absolute skill differences in production.
Gains arise from differences in opportunity cost.

mc.ex: Each instance carries its own attribute copy, while methods defined by the class are shared by every instance. The reversed view incorrectly makes attributes shared and methods separately copied.
